edges.effect_quant: Older cohort studies in dementia consistently show excess mortality with antipsychotic exposure, especially at higher doses and with conventional agents. A 2009 nursing-home cohort found higher death rates with conventional antipsychotics than atypicals, and later dementia cohorts continued to show elevated risk for several commonly used agents, though quetiapine often appears somewhat less harmful than haloperidol or risperidone.
edges.population: older adults with dementia receiving antipsychotics for behavioral or neuropsychiatric symptoms in community or nursing-home settings
edges.mechanism: Antipsychotic use in dementia may increase mortality through sedation, aspiration, stroke, arrhythmia, infections, immobility, and dose-related frailty acceleration in already vulnerable patients. The danger is not only the molecule itself but the combination of cardiovascular, neurologic, and infectious stress imposed on a fragile brain-body system.
edges.summary: Antipsychotic use in dementia is associated with higher mortality, especially with conventional drugs and higher dosing intensity. The precise risk varies by agent and population, but multiple cohort studies now support the basic clinical warning that these drugs can shorten life in people with dementia even when they sometimes reduce severe behavioral symptoms.
edges.caveats: Confounding by indication remains important because the sickest or most behaviorally disturbed dementia patients are also the most likely to receive antipsychotics. Even so, the consistency of dose- and class-related mortality signals is why the black-box concern has persisted rather than fading with time.
